summary: Explains how devices on an ATM network can use ILMI to learn the ATM address of an NHRP server, which helps find shortcut paths, with no manual setup.

plainLanguage.summary: A traveler asks a guide for the nearest map office instead of memorizing where it is. The network switch plays the guide.

questions: how to find an nhrp server
how does nhrp server discovery work
what is the atm service registry mib
how does a diskless host find an nhrp server
subtitle: How an ATM host or router asks its switch where the NHRP server is, instead of being told by hand.

tldr.problem: Configuring a host or router to use NHRP needs at least one ATM address set by hand on every device, and a diskless host cannot be configured locally at all.
tldr.mechanism: The device queries the ATM switch's ILMI Service Registry MIB with SNMP GetNext, sweeping the rows for the NHRP service identifier and picking the row that matches its own network.
tldr.outcome: NHRP clients can find their Next Hop Servers automatically, with the primary server being the row with the lowest index and later rows acting as backups.

today: RFC 2603 is a Proposed Standard published in June 1999. The unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Configuration Problem
sections.content:
Setting up a host or router to use NHRP (the NBMA Next Hop Resolution Protocol, RFC 2332) is described as cumbersome and error-prone. At least one ATM address has to be statically configured on every host or router in the network.

It also rules out some machines entirely: a diskless host cannot use NHRP, because NHRP would need local configuration. ILMI-based Server Discovery (called "server discovery" in the memo) lets ATM-attached hosts and routers learn the ATM addresses of servers dynamically. This RFC defines how that method is used to locate NHRP servers.
sections.plainLanguage: Writing the server's address on every computer by hand is slow and easy to get wrong. This memo lets the computers just ask the network where to go.

sections.title: ILMI and the Service Registry
sections.content:
The Integrated Local Management Interface (ILMI) lets ATM-attached devices such as hosts, routers and ATM switches exchange management information. It is based on SNMP version 1 and supports get, get-next, set and trap operations.

ILMI calls the switch side of an ATM link the network side and the host or router side the user side. The Service Registry MIB, defined by the ATM Forum in ILMI Specification Version 4.0, is implemented on the network side and queried from the user side. To support the existing framework for IP over ATM, ATM switches must support it.
sections.plainLanguage: The switch keeps a phone book of services. Computers on the user side are allowed to look things up in it.

sections.title: The Service Registry Table
sections.content:
Each row of the service registry table has five fields: atmfSrvcRegPort, atmfSrvcRegServiceID, atmfSrvcRegATMAddress, atmfSrvcRegAddressIndex and atmfSrvcRegParm1. The table is indexed by port, service ID and address index.

The service ID is an object identifier naming the type of service. For NHRP it is atmfSrvcRegNHRP, 1.3.6.1.4.1.353.1.5.5. It names no managed objects; it is only used to find the right rows. The address field holds the full ATM address that a client uses to connect to the service. The address index is an arbitrary integer that tells apart several addresses for the same service on the same port. A port of zero means the ATM interface over which the request arrived.

The atmfSrvcRegParm1 octet string is a generic parameter string whose meaning depends on the service ID. For NHRP, to match RFC 2332, it carries the protocol type (16 bits), an optional extension (40 bits), the length of the protocol address (8 bits), the network address and the network mask. For IPv4 the type is 0x0800 and the length is 4; for IPv6 the type is 0x86DD and the length is 16. Addresses and masks are in network byte order.
sections.plainLanguage: Each row is like a card in the phone book: what kind of service, its address, and which network it serves.

sections.title: Next Hop Client Behavior
sections.content:
A Next Hop Client (NHC) reads the table with the SNMP GetNext operator, a linear "sweep" that starts at port 0, the NHRP service ID and index 0, while holding the port and service ID constant.

What the client does with the rows depends on how it is configured. An NHC with no local configuration, such as a diskless workstation, must use the row with the lowest index value when several Next Hop Servers (NHS), possibly for multiple networks, are listed. An NHC with local IP configuration must use a row that has the appropriate IP address. The RFC's example is a router with three logical interfaces (1.0.0.1/8, 128.10.0.1/16 and 171.69.150.226/24) that looks for three matching atmfSrvcRegParm1 values, one per network.

Once it finds the right row, the router may set up an SVC to the chosen NHS and carry on with the normal protocol operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The computer reads down the phone book until it finds the card for its own neighborhood, then calls that number.

sections.title: Redundancy and Server Behavior
sections.content:
Several rows can list several servers. The list is ordered, and the primary NHS has the lowest index value. The NHC must try the primary before using a secondary NHS. Administrators must make sure the listed servers are synchronized.

An NHS itself is locally configured. It may read the NHRP service registry data to check the results, and if it finds an incorrect row it may flag the error in a locally significant way.

The RFC also notes that the ATM Forum's PNNI Augmented Routing (PAR), and a proxy mechanism for it, could be used to manage the registry tables on switches. Hosts and routers would keep using the same discovery mechanism, so nothing in this memo would need to change.
sections.plainLanguage: If the first number is busy, the computer tries the next card in order. The helpers on the list have to know the same things.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Server discovery relies on the security of the ILMI management framework. Access to user-side or network-side information is controlled by the design of the MIB rather than by protocol security mechanisms.

The service registry MIB is defined with read-only access. Any user-side device may query the registry, but cannot change it over ILMI. Changes have to be made by local configuration on the ATM switch.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone can read the phone book, but only the people who run the switch can write in it.

fields.name: ar$pro.type
fields.desc: Protocol type; IPv4 is 0x0800, IPv6 is 0x86DD.

fields.name: ar$pro.snap
fields.desc: Optional extension to protocol type; 0 for IPv4 and IPv6.

fields.name: ar$plen
fields.desc: Length of the protocol address; 4 for IPv4, 16 for IPv6.
